questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

So, let $u=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $-1$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)$ | $1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1)} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem:

\displaystyle \int \frac{2\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2}\,\text{d}x.
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2}\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\text{d}u) \\  & =-2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{csc}⁡x+2|+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem:

\displaystyle \int \frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})}\,\text{d}y.
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}))=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}).
$$

So, let $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2}).$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=2y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u=y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})\,\text{d}y.
$$

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})}\cdot (y\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{2}))\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡({y}^{2})|+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.:question/problem:
Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\,\text{d}x.
$$
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,\text{d}u={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}(u-1)\text{d}u \\  & =\int (1-\frac{1}{u})\,\text{d}u \\  & =u-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =(\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1|+C \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1|+K\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=C+1.$

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=2 \tan{\left(x \right)} \sec{\left(x \right)}.

$$

$$

The transformed integral is

$$
\int \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u.
$$

$$

$$

Substitute back:

$$
-2\left(\ln\left|\cot{\left(x \right)} + 3\right|\right)+C.
$$

questions.:question/problem:
Evaluate exactly.

$$
\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{3 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\cos^{3}{\left(x \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

You may use $\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C$.

Endpoint values: $\cos{\left(0 \right)}=1,\quad \cos{\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \right)}=0$.

{{answer}}
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\cos^{3}{\left(x \right)} + 2$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=- 3 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Transform both bounds:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=0&\Longrightarrow u=3\\x=\frac{\pi}{2}&\Longrightarrow u=2\end{aligned}
$$

The new bounds decrease. Keep this order when evaluating the antiderivative.

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{3 \sin{\left(x \right)} \cos^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\cos^{3}{\left(x \right)} + 2}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=-\left(\int_{3}^{2} \frac{1}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u\right).\end{aligned}
$$

Both transformed bounds are positive. Evaluating gives

$$
-\left(\left[\ln u\right]_{3}^{2}\right)=-\left(\ln\left(2\right)-\ln\left(3\right)\right).
$$

The answer is

$$
-\left(\ln\left(2\right)-\ln\left(3\right)\right).
$$

\int \frac{\tan{\left(x \right)} \sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3}\,\mathrm{d}x
$$

You may use $\int 1/u\,\mathrm{d}u=\ln\left|u\right|+C$.

questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $u=\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3$. Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x}=\tan{\left(x \right)} \sec{\left(x \right)}.
$$

Since $\sec{\left(x \right)}=u-3$, rewrite the remaining factor:

$$
\frac{u-3}{u}=1-\frac{3}{u}.
$$

Including the differential factor gives

$$
\begin{aligned}&\int \frac{\tan{\left(x \right)} \sec^{2}{\left(x \right)}}{\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3}\,\mathrm{d}x\\&=\int 1 - \frac{3}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:

$$
\int 1 - \frac{3}{u}\,\mathrm{d}u=u-3\left(\ln\left|u\right|\right)+C.
$$

Substitute back:

$$
\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3-3\left(\ln\left|\sec{\left(x \right)} + 3\right|\right)+C.
$$

\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1+\tan^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$
canonical_example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.
$$

So, let $u = 1+\tan^2 x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi/4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$
